question: What can the U.S. block or decide in each international body, and what can't it?
answer: Across 27 bodies, U.S. power sits in five different places: a veto, consensus seat or blocking share in 5 (United Nations, NATO, International Monetary Fund, ITER, Board of Peace), money leverage in 8, domestic implementation in 8, command or facility access in 5 and agenda power in 6. A gate can stop specified action but does not give command: at the UN Security Council, procedural matters require nine votes and are not vetoable; affirmative action still needs nine votes.

sections.title: The five places U.S. power sits

items.label: Constitutional gates
items.note: A veto, consensus seat, blocking share or unanimity right can stop specified action without conferring unilateral command.

items.label: Money leverage
items.note: Assessment, capital, quota, replenishment and voluntary-donor power use different denominators and legal effects.

items.label: Domestic implementation
items.note: The international body owns a common rule or record; U.S. agencies and law determine domestic effect.

items.label: Command & facility access
items.note: Command, inspection, hardware, project committees and data access are operating rights, not generic membership.

items.label: Agenda & coalition power
items.note: Forums and accords align priorities and route work, while downstream legal owners still must act.

sections.title: At the United Nations: what the U.S. can and cannot do
sections.sub: The ten U.S. roles on the UN chart, each with its legal basis.

rows.text: Charter member
rows.note: United Nations · legal basis: UN Charter; U.S. ratification; United Nations Participation Act.

rows.text: One General Assembly vote and full participation in open Member-State organs. Drafting, sponsorship, diplomacy, coalition building and implementation capacity.
No general veto outside the Security Council; one country cannot command the Organization.
Permanent Security Council member
rows.note: Security Council · legal basis: Charter Articles 23 and 27; Council voting practice.

rows.text: Permanent seat and veto over substantive Council decisions under Article 27 practice. Agenda, drafting, sanctions, mandate renewals and Secretary-General recommendation.
Procedural matters require nine votes and are not vetoable; affirmative action still needs nine votes.
Headquarters host State
rows.note: New York headquarters district · legal basis: 1947 Headquarters Agreement; 1946 General Convention.

rows.text: Domestic sovereign responsibilities coexist with treaty duties to enable UN functions, access and privileges. Security, visas, infrastructure and host-country administration affect daily operation.
Host status is not an extra vote or a power to direct UN deliberations.
Largest regular-budget assessment
rows.note: General Assembly / Fifth Committee · legal basis: A/RES/79/249 and annual assessment letters.

rows.text: No extra vote from paying more. At the adopted 22% cap for 2025–2027, U.S. payment timing and budget positions materially affect liquidity and negotiations.
Assessment is a collective legal obligation under Article 17, not ownership equity.
Largest peacekeeping assessment
rows.note: Security Council + General Assembly budget route · legal basis: A/RES/79/250 and A/79/318/Add.1.

rows.text: Mandate vote as P5 and separate one-country vote in the Assembly budget process. The effective U.S. rate is 26.1371% for 2026 because P5 members pay a premium.
A Council mandate and an Assembly appropriation remain separate decisions; U.S. law governs payment.
Voluntary donor and programme partner
rows.note: Funds, programmes and field operations · legal basis: Entity board decisions, contribution agreements and appropriations.

rows.text: Rights come from governing-board membership and contribution agreements, not donation size alone. Earmarking, scale, technical expertise, procurement and country partnerships can shape implementation.
Voluntary funding cannot lawfully rewrite a governing body's mandate.
Nomination, election and appointment actor
rows.note: GA, SC, ECOSOC and agency organs · legal basis: Charter Article 97; ICJ Statute; body-specific rules.

rows.text: Votes in elections and nominates U.S. candidates where rules permit. Campaigning, regional bargains and P5 leverage in Secretary-General recommendations.
A U.S. national elected in an independent capacity is not automatically a U.S. delegate.
Domestic authorization and appropriations gate
rows.note: President, State Department and Congress · legal basis: 22 U.S.C. §§287–287a and annual statutes.

rows.text: The President directs U.S. representatives through the Secretary of State; Congress enacts appropriations and implementing law. Domestic funding, sanctions, treaty implementation and agency authorities determine what the United States can deliver.
Domestic law does not by itself amend the UN Charter or another organization's constitution.
Member of autonomous agencies
rows.note: WHO, UNESCO, FAO, ITU, ILO and others · legal basis: Each agency's constitution and relationship agreement.

rows.text: Usually one-state/one-vote plus eligibility for executive organs under each constitution. Contributions, expertise, standards bodies and executive-board seats.
UN Security Council or General Assembly status does not carry over automatically.
Weighted shareholder
rows.note: IMF and World Bank · legal basis: IMF and IBRD Articles of Agreement.

rows.text: Quota/capital-based votes rather than one-country/one-vote. The U.S. IMF share can block decisions requiring 85% of total voting power; IBRD influence derives from shareholding.
These institutions are autonomous; UNGA cannot direct their loans or votes.

uncertain: The five places are an interpretive grouping by the International Organizations map (source status: interpretive grouping, see registry), not a legal category.

This is a United States relationship and control map, not a complete history of every organization. Organizations, organs, programmes, treaty regimes, forums, facilities and accords remain separately typed. Institution-specific percentages use different denominators and cannot be consolidated. Exit, defunding, internal refit, parallel doctrine, shared machinery, resource migration, default use and residual-incumbent status remain separate states.
Records read: registry as of October 4, 2026; UN chart as of September 20, 2026.
